summary: A humorous April 1st RFC that proposes a framework for detecting sarcasm in AI systems and guidelines for using sarcasm without offending. It is a joke, not a real specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9405 is an April 1st proposal for detecting sarcasm in AI systems. It describes labeled training examples, text features, and security concerns in a serious technical style.

questions: what is the ai sarcasm detection protocol
how does the rfc propose detecting sarcasm
subtitle: An April 1st framework proposes training AI systems to identify sarcasm.

tldr.problem: Sarcasm depends on context and tone, which can make it difficult for an AI system to interpret.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9405 proposes a sarcasm-detection framework using labeled examples and an algorithm that extracts linguistic and contextual features before classification.
tldr.outcome: The RFC presents the proposal in a humorous April 1st document. It also lists risks from adversarial input, sensitive training data, and malicious use.

today: RFC 9405 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2023. It presents a humorous framework for sarcasm detection and discusses security and privacy risks.

sections.title: Why Sarcasm Is Difficult to Interpret
sections.content: The RFC describes sarcasm as language that uses irony and may say the opposite of what is intended. It notes that context and tone matter, which can make sarcasm difficult for AI systems to detect. It presents the issue and its proposed framework with a lighthearted tone.
sections.plainLanguage: Sarcasm can use words whose literal meaning differs from the speaker's intention. The RFC jokes about a technical method for helping AI recognize it.

sections.title: Training Data and Classification
sections.content: The proposed AI Sarcasm Detection Protocol has two main parts: training data and a detection algorithm. The RFC says the data should contain diverse sarcastic and non-sarcastic samples with labels. An algorithm can tokenize text, extract features such as irony or contextual cues, and classify the input.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal starts with examples labeled as sarcastic or not. An algorithm looks for language patterns and context, then classifies new text.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content: The RFC lists adversarial attacks that may produce false classifications, privacy risks if training data contains personal information, and malicious use to manipulate people. It recommends protecting requests and responses with secure communication protocols and protecting the training data from unauthorized access.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers could mislead the classifier, and training data may contain private details. The RFC says to protect both the data and the communication.
